US Army to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa after Trump paused plan
- Published
The US military has said it will move forward with plans to detonate five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa after an appeals court cleared the way.
The plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound that is reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were put on pause earlier in the day after US President Donald Trump ordered the Army to not move ahead unless a court and the state's incoming governor agreed.
The plans have faced legal challenges and public outcry over potential health and environmental hazards.
Army Secretary Adam Telle made the announcement late Monday that the military would detonate the explosives on Wednesday morning, calling it a "consensus decision".
"Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa's current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts," Telle said. "We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa's citizens comes first."
His announcement came shortly after the 8th Circuit US Court of Appeals ruled that the plans could move forward, finding there were an emergency reason and adequate safeguards in place.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, has argued it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
Earlier in the day, Trump said he felt the "proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until" both the courts and the state's incoming governor Rob Sand agreed.
Sand, a Democrat, will not lead the state until January when he's sworn into office, has not said whether he agreed with the military's plan. The current governor of the state is Republican Kim Reynolds.
Before the court ruling, Sand urged the Trump administration to be transparent and share information publicly that he's received in private briefings. He said Iowans are entitled to know how they "came to this situation" and why "this is the best path forward".
The Army Secretary noted in his announcement that current Gov Reynolds "has given her support to go forward".
A court had previously ordered a pause on the plan after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, which was originally scheduled for last Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown.
Even after the pause was put in place, the justice department told the court that the Army intended to move forward because of an "immediate risk" that the munitions could "spontaneously explode".
Environmental groups have accused the federal government of skirting the judicial process.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move it, according to Iowa Public Radio.
The EPA says no level of lead exposure is considered safe. Lead exposure through inhalation or ingestion can pose serious health risks to humans and animals, particularly children.
The 8th Circuit US Court of Appeals said in its order on Monday night that the EPA adequately included safeguards in the emergency permit to minimise dust dispersal to address safety concerns.
The US Army has said it planned to carry out the detonation on Wednesday to allow for "optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced". Telle said those plans are set for Wednesday morning at the plant.
Middletown's Mayor Rodney Johnson on Monday backed the detonation and said it "must take place".
"It doesn't matter who dropped the ball on the removal of these expired munitions, the ball is now in November 2026 Court," Johnson said in a statement. "The buzzer is ticking and if we don't take this opportunity to safely dispose of the problem, then actual lives may be at stake !!!"
He added that "every possible precaution" had been put into place to ensure people's safety.
The government has argued that, because this is an event that requires immediate action, the Army can move forward without a permit for detonation.
The justice department's court filing describes this as an "emergency situation" in part because of the incoming cold weather.
"As the outside temperatures drop the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures," the filing said.
It said that a controlled detonation would protect the public from the possibly greater dangers in an unplanned explosion.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed the legal case on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause.
"Despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau, who is representing the groups.
